Document Text: Date: 14/02/2024 Ref: CAM6854 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 17/01/2024 about the number of temporary accommodation properties, average length of stay and cost per night. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested. However, we are withholding all of the information because it is exempt as explained below. We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply. Please see the refusal notic es at the end of the questions which explain how and why they apply. 1. How many properties do you currently have on temporary accommodation in 2024? How many did you have in 2019? How many did you have in 2014? How many in 2010? How many in 2005? How many in 2000? 2. How many households do you have in hotels (- e.g. Travelodge, Premier Inn etc) in temporary accommodation, as of now, 2019 and 2014? 3. Please send a list, with as much information as you can provide with the names of the hotels you are using for temporary accommodation, including the rates you are paying per room and the length of stay of these families in this accommodation. 4. How many households are on the waiting list for permanent housing? 5. How many households are waiting to be moved into temporary accommodation? 6. How long do households stay, on average, in hotels, on a temporary accommodation basis? 7. How much are you currently paying in the hotels, per room, per night on average, to re-house a household? 8. How much does the nightly rate differ for single, double and triple bedrooms, in a hotel? (E.g., Travelodge, Premier Inn etc). For example, a family of four who would take 2 rooms in a hotel room - how much are you paying per night per room for them, on average? 9. What is the minimum and maximum you currently pay for a hotel room to relocate a household/family? London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk 10. Please can you advise us on the MAXIMUM that your council CURRENTLY pays, per night for a: Studio, 1 Bed, 2 Bed, 3 Bed & 4 Bed in temporary accommodation nightly rate bookings. Please include the maximum rates for properties that you are currently paying, including that which is paid OVER your advertised rates. There is no way Pan-London/LHA rates are viable for any landlord so we would like to know how much you ACTUALLY are paying for your highly demanded temporary accommodation units. 11. Please can you advise us on the MAXIMUM that your council CURRENTLY pays per room for a HMO, on a nightly temporary accommodation basis? How do rates differ for self-contained units to shared amenity units? Please send a list of nightly rates. Please include the rates for properties that you are currently paying, including that which is paid over your advertised rates. There is no way Pan - London/LHA rates are viable for any landlord so we would like to know how much you ACTUALLY are paying for your highly demanded temporary accommodation units. 12. What is the average length of stay in HMO accommodation, on a temporary accommodation basis? 13. What is the MAXIMUM you CURRENTLY pay per night for hostels and Bed and Breakfasts for Studio, 1 Bed, 2 Bed, 3 Bed & 4 Bed property, in temporary accommodation? How does this differ for self-contained units? How much per room? Please include the rates for properties that you are currently paying, including that which is paid over your advertised rates. There is no way Pan -London rates are viable for any landlord so we would like to know how much you ACTUALLY are paying for your highly demanded temporary accommodation units. 14. What is the average length of stay in Hostels and Bed and breakfast accommodation, on a temporary accommodation basis? 15. Who are your largest 30 suppliers for temporary accommodation? Please send us a list and include hotels. 16. How many properties have they given you? 17. How much do you pay them, per year, for these properties? 18. If we were to supply nightly paid temporary accommodation on this basis, please can you give us all the available information you have for their: CONTACT NAMES, JOB DESCRIPTIONS and TELEPHONE NUMBERS (e.g. direct dials/extension numbers) of the procurement team(s) so we can get the ball rolling as soon as possible. This should include the email and phone numbers for the “head of housing,” “head of temporary accommodation,” “temporary accommodation team leader,” “temporary accommodation officer” and “decant officer”. 19. How many people and families are on the waiting list for temporary accommodation/decent housing in 2024? How many were on the waiting list for temporary housing in 2019? 20. What is the average length of stay for a temporary accommodation tenant, in a private-rented-sector unit. E.g., A house procurement from a private landlord by your Council? What is the average length of stay for a temporary accommodation tenant, in a hotel room? 21. How often, on average, are tenants moved from one t emporary accommodation unit to another? 22. How many of your tenants are rehoused in each of the 32 London boroughs - on a temporary accommodation (and hostel) nightly paid basis? (If you do not have data for the 32, the top 10 is sufficient). 23. Does your council utilize decant (relocation) housing? If so, please can you give us all the available information you have for their: CONTACT NAMES, JOB DESCRIPTIONS and TELEPHONE NUMBERS (e.g. direct dials/extension numbers) of the procurement team(s) so we can get the ball rolling as soon as possible. 24. Please send me the department email and phone number for asylum seeker placements, outside of the home-office remit. For example, the re-housing for Ukrainian Families. 25. What is the max, min and average you are currently paying on for emergency decant housing, for different unit sizes, 1-6 bed property for example? E.g. Family of four emergency relocation into a four bedroom house, procuring a property from the Private rented sector, on a nightly let, emergency basis. 26. Please send a list of the top 10 housing associations you use to assist in Decanting your residents from one place to another, in temporary accommodation. 27. How much do you currently pay, on average, for a 3 bed temporary accommodation home on a nightly rate? How much do you currently pay for a 2 bed temporary accommodation unit on a nightly rate? 28. Does your council do “nightly rate block booking” for your temporary accommodation placement. This is temporary accommodation housing, which is paid on a nightly rate basis, that is block booked throughout a given period - e.g., 12 months - 5 years. Refusal notice: The exemption that applies is: Section 12: Cost of Compliance Exceeds the Appropriate Limit We are refusing your request under section 12 on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit". This is £450 which is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the requester. Once the council has ascertained that the appropriate limit will be reached it does not need to estimate the time that would be needed for the remainder of the request . There is no obligation on the council to work on a request until the 18 hours limit is reached, o nce it is reasonably calculated that the limit will be reached the entire request may be refused. The information you are seeking for Q8, Q9 and Q11 is not readily available because the agreements for determining the rates applied to the procurement of temporary accommodation in London is complex. The Local Housing Allowance (LHA) rate given for a household is the starting point for determining the cost of placing a household in temporary accommodation. The rates vary for each household according to the size and location of their temporary accommodation and is set nationally by the Valuation Office Agency (VOA) . Camden is one of the boroughs that has committed to procure temporary accommodation at the Pan- London rates, in line with the Inter Borough Accommodation Agreement (IBAA) administered by the West London Alliance. The VOA divides London into a geography of Broad Rental Market Areas (BRMA), each having different rates for temporary accommodation that cuts across borough boundaries. The IBAA procurement agreement allows each borough to pay slightly different rates for properties in the same BRMA. To calculate the maximum rate of each placement would require the creation of a data set for analysis by a council officer. It is estimated to extract and review the data for a single record would take approx. 5 minutes. To complete the task for all 700 households in temporary accommodation would take approx. 58 hours, this greatly exceeds the 18 hours required by the Act. Advice and Assistance: Given the calculations above, it would be difficult to refine the request so that it would take less than the time limit. We do have the answer to some questions and have provided this below by way of advice and assistance. Regarding Q2, we hold some of the information. From 2019/20 onwards quarterly information on temporary accommodation is publicly available. You can view the data through the Department of Levelling Up, Housing and Communities link: https://www.gov.uk/government/statistical-data-sets/live-tables-on-homelessness . The data for all local authorities is provided in separate files for each quarter described as 'Detailed local authority level tables'. Within each file, the sheet labelled TA1 has a breakdown of the number of households by temporary accommodation type and also includes the number of children. As the information requested is already reasonably accessible elsewhere it is exempt under the absolute exemption in Section 21 In response to Q4 on 31 January 2023, there were 7,035 households waiting to be housed by the London Borough of Camden. For Q5 and Q19, we do not hold or maintain a waiting list for temporary accommodation. Regarding Q23 and Q24, Camden does not use decant housing Further Information: We do not give our consent for any names and contact details provided in this response to be sent marketing material. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000.  Response The council holds the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: 1.         A summary of any housing stock transfer(s) undertaken by the council in the past, including the names of the housing association(s) and the year(s) of transfer 2.         A copy/copies of the transfer agreement(s) for any stock transfers 3.         If known, a summary of commitments made by the receiving housing association(s) for investment in the stock being transferred (e.g. £50m over 10 years) 4.         If known, a summary of commitments made by the receiving housing association(s) for development of affordable housing (e.g. 200 new affordable homes over 5 years) 5.         The council’s understanding of the amount invested in the stock by the housing association in the years following the transfer, and whether this part of the agreement was met 6.         The council’s understanding of the number of affordable homes delivered by the housing association in the local authority area in the years following the transfer, and whether this part of the agreement was met 7.         The amount of money received by the council as part of the stock transfer(s) 8.         A summary of how the council spent the money received through the stock transfer(s) Housing stock transfer was introduced by government in 1988 and is the voluntary transfer of ownership of all or some of a local authority's tenanted and leasehold homes to either a housing association specifically created for that purpose or an already existing housing association. Under the terms of such transfers, which were captured in a transfer agreement, the receiving housing associations have undertaken to carry out property repairs and modernisation, including implementation of the Decent Homes Standard once this was officially prescribed by government in 2000. Some transfers have also included commitments from the receiving housing association for development of affordable housing. Whilst the Council did sell or lease some stock to housing associations in the 1980s and 1990s, it has never carried out any stock transfer of the type described above.  Further Information: We do not give our consent for any names and contact details provided in this response to be sent marketing material. Date: 31/07/2020 Ref: CAM247 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 16/07/2020 about Disabled Persons Parking Badges. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: I make a formal Freedom of Information Request concerning Camden Council’s implementation of the Department for Transports Guidance on the issuing of Disabled Persons Parking Badges, as per the link provided by yourselves: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/blue - badge-can-i-get-one/can-i-get-a-blue-badge Specifically, you have provided a link to the DFT Guidance, the question relates to your implementation of the Guidance. Date: 15/12/2025 Case reference: CAM11626 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 21/11/2025 about properties exempt from Council Tax.  We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested.  However, we are withholding the information because it is exempt as explained below.  We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemption applies.  Please see the refusal notice at the end of the answer which explains how and why it applies.  I am writing to request information under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. I am seeking data relating to properties within your authority area that are currently exempt from Council Tax under the following classes: • Class E – Property left empty where the liable person is in hospital. • Class F – Property left empty following the death of the liable person. Specifically, I request: 1. Please provide the number of properties in each full postcode (not just the outward or first-half code) where either Class E or Class F exemptions are applied. Purpose and Public InterestThis request is made in the public interest. I am conducting research to: • Understand housing availability and long-term vacancy patterns in the local area. • Track the extent to which properties remain empty during the probate process, which can inform local and national housing policy. Empty homes are a matter of national concern, and greater transparency on exemption data will help inform evidence-based policy solutions. Crime Risk and Mitigation I am aware of refusals under Section 31(1)(a) (prevention of crime). I respectfully submit that: • My request does not seek full property addresses, only aggregated postcode-level counts, eliminating the risk of properties being individually identified. • Classes E and F typically relate to properties under legal control (executors or solicitors), which are no more vulnerable than those already published through Land Registry data. • Aggregated data poses no realistic risk of unauthorised occupation or criminal activity. I am happy for the data to be provided in spreadsheet (Excel or CSV) format if possible. This information is exempt.  Please see the exemption notice set out below. Refusal Notice The exemption that applies is: section 31(1)(a) – Law Enforcement We do not release the exact postcodes of empty properties.  Information released under the FOIA is not just sent to the requester but is effectively published to the world at large.The exact postcodes would allow squatters or criminals to identify the empty properties this is particularly the case in areas where there may be a higher number of empty properties or there are only a few number of properties to search to find an empty property. We consider disclosing this information would make empty properties a target of crime. Therefore, this information is exempt from disclosure under section 31(1)(a) of the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Section 31(1)(a) says that we do not need to provide information that would be likely to prejudice the functions of law enforcement- the prevention and detection of crime. Camden believes that releasing this information would increase the likelihood of : Empty properties being lived in by squatters. Squatting in a residential property is now a criminal offence. • Empty properties being targeted by vandals or graffiti artists and stripped of materials such as roofing, cables or piping, or otherwise vandalised or damaged. • Empty properties being targeted by criminals or terrorists for example allowing them to hide or store the proceeds of crime, or criminal or terrorist materials • In the Information Tribunal Case Yiannis Voyias v Information Commissioner and the London Borough of Camden (EA/2001/0007 23 January 2013) the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) (the “Tribunal”) upheld Camden’s decision to withhold the addresses of empty houses under section 31(1)(a). This approach has been followed by both the Information Commissioner (ICO) and other First Tier Tribunal Decisions. For example: In 2019 the First Tier Tribunal (EA/2018/0055) upheld Sheffield City Council’s decision to apply s31(1)(a) to the information. • In 2029 the ICO Decision Notice FS50786336 upheld London Borough of Hackney’s decision to apply s31(1)(a) to the information • In 2022/3 the First Tier Tribunal upheld the ICO’s decision to uphold London Borough of Hounslow’s decision to withhold the information under s31(1)(a) • In 2024 the ICO Decision Notice IC-274382-J3Y0 upheld Newark and Sherwood District Council’s decision to withhold the information under s31(1)(a). • The law is settled on this point. Public Interest Test: As Section 31 is a qualified exemption we need to consider the public interest test. Factors in favour of disclosure There are general arguments in promoting transparency and accountability of public authorities.• Raising the profile of vacant properties would help encourage public engagement and debate.• Factors in favour of withholding There is an inherent public interest in crime prevention. This was considered in the Voyias case by the Tribunal. • There is public interest in avoiding the costs associated with squatting, for example repair, security and eviction costs. • The negative impact of squatting affects the surrounding community and public authorities involved, not just the individual property •  We believe that the balance of public interest lies in upholding the exemption and not releasing the information. This decision has been consistently upheld by the ICO and the First Tier Tribunal. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: 1.What is the number of drug and alcohol rehabilitation placements funded for adults by the local authority as at 1.1.22? In 2019/20 - 36 Camden residents accessed residential treatment funded by the LA. In 2020/21- 20 Camden residents accessed residential treatment funded by the LA. Please note this is lower than 2019/20 due to the impact of COVID on residential provider’s ability to accept admissions. So far in 2021/22 (up until Oct 21) 8 Camden residents have accessed residential treatment funded by the LA. Data for October onwards is currently unavailable. 2.  Are local authority drug and alcohol rehab placements means tested for each individual that come to the attention of the LA? If so what are the benchmarks used to assess whether an adult requires the local authorities support with funding a drug and alcohol rehabilitation placement.  Each individual is financially assessed by the Assessments & Adult Social Care Income team within the council to ascertain if client contribution is required.  3. Do the local authority fund drug and alcohol rehab placements for individuals if directed by the judicial system that it would better suit an offenders needs over incarceration?  All referrals are considered including those either in or leaving the criminal justice system.  4. What is the percentage increase in local authority funded drug and alcohol rehabilitation placements for the financial years of 2019/20 to 2020/21.  The budget for residential treatment sits within Public Health.  The budget for residential treatment is as follows: 2019-20       £400,000 2020-21       £400,000 5. What is the proportion of adults that pay for drug and alcohol rehabilitation placements privately that come to the local authorities attention? We do not hold data on those who fund their residential treatment privately.  6.  Is there an internal panel consultation process to decide whether the local authority will fund a drug and alcohol rehabilitation placement? What are the parameters for approving or declining a placement?  Yes there is a panel process.  Each individual is assessed on their own personal circumstances, there is usually an expectation that individuals will have engaged with community services prior to referral for residential treatment. 7. Are drug and alcohol rehabilitation placements ultimately funded by the NHS once approved by the local authority? As per response to question 4.  The funding for the residential treatment comes from the local authorities Public Health budget. 8. Which department handles drug and alcohol rehabilitation issues for adults? Public Health 9. Do you have a preferred provider list or approved framework of drug and alcohol rehabilitation clinics and/or treatment centres? Yes we have framework contract of approved detox and residential rehab providers. 10. What are the requirements for becoming an approved provider or part of an approved framework? This is managed through a tender process whereby providers need to provide evidence that they can provide services safely and effectively, and have appropriate clinical and therapeutic protocols andstandards.  They have to be CQC registered, and be able to adhere to data collection and monitoring processes. 11.  What was the average length of a drug and alcohol rehabilitation placement funded by the local authority for the financial year 2019/20. This varies and is agreed on an individual basis.  Most detox placements have an average length of 2 weeks, and an initial rehab placement will be 12 weeks.  However, clients are able to request a further 12 weeks if they feel it is required, this is usually agreed at the 8 week review point. 12. What is the current cost of each individual drug and alcohol rehabilitation placement funded by the local authority for adults as at 1.1.22 and what is the length of each placement? Costs of placements vary depending on client need.  An average 12 week rehab stay would cost approx. £8,500, if the client presents with complex needs and requires more intensive support an average 12 week stay would be approx. £12,000.  The average length of each placement varies, as per response to Q11, each placement starts with a 12 week stay. However, some people may not finish their 12 week placement and leave rehab earlier than anticipated.  If this is the case, individuals are either supported by community services or an alternative rehab placements are explored with the individual.  Further Information: We do not give our consent for any names and contact details provided in this response to be sent marketing material. Document Text: Date: 19/12/2023 Ref: CAM6510 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 20/11/2023 about Safer & Stronger Communities Funding allocations to LSP between 2006 -2010. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The Council does not hold the information requested. The answer to your questions is as follows: Regarding the award to your local authority of £1.6 million of government funding of the Neighbourhood Element of the Safer and Stronger Communities Fund (SSCF NE), over four years from 2006 to 2010. The Safer and Stronger Communities Fund brought together various government funding streams with the aim of tackling crime and anti -social behaviour, empowering communities and improving the public realm, with the SSCF NE targeted at the most disadvantaged neighbourhoods, i.e., the 3% most deprived Lower Layer Super Output Areas (LSOAs) as measured by the Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD). Funding under the Neighbourhood Element was to be allocated by Local Strategic Partnerships (LSPs), within the framework of Local Area Agreements, where they existed, and was designed to support LSPs in promoting community safety, liveability and community engagement in the most disadvantaged neighbourhoods, through initiatives such as a neighbourhood management arra ngements. Could you please provide me in electronic form, e.g. Word document or PDFs, of: i) Confirmation that the local authority/LSP was awarded funding under the SSCF NE, and how much it was awarded. ii) Which LSOAs in the local authority area received the SSCF NE ( i.e., LSOA identification numbers at the time of the award) London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk iii) Documentation agreed with the regional Government Office outlining how the SSCF NE was going to be spent iv) Details of the neighbourhood management arrangements introduced under the SSCF NE v) The report of the mandatory local resident evidence baseline survey commissioned by the local authority/LSP in the LSOAs which received SSCF NE funding at the commencement of the award (likely to be 2006) vi) The final report of the mandatory local resident baseline survey commissioned by the local authority/LSP in the LSOAs which received SSCF NE funding towards the mid or end point of the award (likely to be 2007/08, 2008/9 or 2009/10) vii) Any evaluations conducted by the local authority/LSP of the performance of the SSCF NE and/or on the introduction of neighbourhood management arrangements, including any other qualitative or quantitative data on its local impact viii) If there is still a LSP for the local authority area ix) if the local authority currently operates neighbourhood management arrangements, details of how and where neighbourhood management operates, and any documents detailing its performance We do not hold this information. These areas are cut once per annum and cutting s are collected and removed from site. A system called WEED-IT (Weed Economical Eradication Detection – Intelligent Technology) is used and this weed control application technology is mounted on the front of a carrier vehicle.
